Lessons.Title: Common Denominators to Compare
ExplanationParagraphs: Source: 2021 Grade 4 Unit 2 Lesson 15. The five-minute opening asks how 15 and 30 are related. Their shared multiples prepare us for using common denominators.

Learning goal: compare two fractions with unlike, non-multiple-related denominators by writing equivalent fractions with a common denominator. Fractions describe the same whole, so equal denominators mean equal-size fractional parts.

Activity 15.1 Tricky Fractions? (20 minutes): first compare 4/3 with 13/12, then 4/3 with 7/5. The second pair requires rewriting both fractions if using a common denominator. Han's proposed limitation is a reasoning prompt, not a ban on converting both fractions.

Discuss Priya and Lin's distinct approaches with a teacher; distinguish mathematically equivalent transformations from unequal-size drawn segments. Explain each result clearly rather than guessing from denominator size.

Activity 15.2 Use a Common Denominator, or Not: construct equivalent representations for 5/6 and 3/4, 2/3 and 5/8, 2/6 and 4/10, 7/4 and 17/10. Students may use equivalent fractions or another valid exact strategy, then explain the comparisons.

Edulytics first-party Cool-down (not the gated publisher source item): justify 7/10<5/7 using a common denominator and an independently checked inequality. Original diagram arguments and any remaining publisher questions stay teacher-reviewed.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent fractions preserve value
KeyConcepts.Definition: Scaling numerator and denominator by the same positive factor changes the representation, not the value.
KeyConcepts.Rule: a/b = (ka)/(kb) for nonzero b and positive k.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common denominator
KeyConcepts.Definition: A denominator shared by two equivalent forms makes equal-sized parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose any common multiple of both denominators, and scale both correctly.

KeyConcepts.Title: Independent fraction comparison
KeyConcepts.Definition: Check a/b versus c/d with positive denominators by comparing ad to bc.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Do not round; exact integer arithmetic preserves close comparisons.

WorkedExamples.Title: When only one fraction needs conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: Is 4/3 or 13/12 larger?

WorkedExamples.Title: When both fractions need conversion
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare 4/3 and 7/5.
Steps: Since 20<21, the second fraction is greater.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source activity 15.2: four comparisons
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare 5/6 to 3/4, 2/3 to 5/8, 2/6 to 4/10, and 7/4 to 17/10.
WorkedExamples.Method: Construct equivalent fractions with shared denominators.

CommonMistakes.Correction: Multiply both numerator and denominator by the same factor.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The fractions' parts are different sizes.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Make common denominators or use cross products of positive denominators.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assuming a greater denominator implies a greater fraction.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Denominator tells partition size, not alone the value.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use exact equivalence and benchmarks or cross multiplication.
